Finally, an AMD ZCU104 FPGA implementation confirms that HDMark adds no hardware overhead, remains bit-exact under aggressive undervolting, and stays verifiable under timing faults until the classifier itself fails.

title: Exact approach to double- and triple-excitation bound state in open quantum systems
authors: X. S. Sun, H. T. Cui, Y. A. Yan, H. Z. Shen
abstract: The determination of multiple-excitation bound state in open quantum systems is of broad interest in quantum physics. While the emergence of double- or triple-excitation bound state has been demonstrated in certain specific situations, their universality and exact solvability remain elusive. In this work, we present an exact approach to the double- or triple-excitation dynamics for interacting quantum emitters coupled to environment by deriving a closed equation. By this exact equation, we identify the critical condition for the emergence of double- or triple-excitation bound state, as well as its relationship to the single-excitation one. Our study not only clearly demonstrates the universality of double- or triple-excitation bound state in open quantum emitter systems, but also reveals the possibility of mediating inter-emitter interactions via multiple-excitation bound states.

title: DELTA: Diagnosing Exploration Lineages via Twin-path Alignment - What Can Contrasting Design Paths Reveal About Microarchitectural Behavior?
authors: Kaushal Mhapsekar, Darsh Asher, Bita Aslrousta, Amna Hassan, Debayan Sengupta, Azam Ghanbari, Samira Mirbagher Ajorpaz
abstract: Architects have two mature instruments for performance work. Top-Down analysis tells them where a design loses its pipeline slots, and design-space exploration (DSE) tells them which configuration scores best. Neither explains why a search stops improving: why a backend-bound design rejects a prefetcher that the bottleneck label recommends, or why a capacity increase that helped in one configuration hurts in the next. This paper argues that the evidence needed to answer such questions is already produced during exploration and then discarded. Every parent-child edge in an exploration tree is a controlled intervention: one knob changes, the rest of the design is held fixed, and a cycle-level simulator measures the outcome. When the same edit helps under one parent and hurts under another, aligning the two parents localizes the interaction that decides its sign. We present DELTA, a simulator-grounded root-cause analysis tool that builds a Design Memory of such interventions during exploration and lets an architect query it afterwards. Each record stores the full parent configuration, the single applied edit, the measured and predicted IPC, a Top-Down breakdown from StallLens, our gem5 implementation of Top-Down, and its lineage. Unlike evolutionary LLM search, which keeps only high-scoring programs, DELTA keeps failed edges as evidence. The same memory also makes exploration efficient: on four SPEC CPU2017 workloads, the full system raises IPC by 55.5% in 22 simulated designs for $1.56 of model cost, predicts the IPC of its own proposals to within 3.3%, and keeps improving after a bottleneck-guided search stalls. A root-cause query over the recorded history led us to a usefulness-throttled variant of the Best-Offset prefetcher that improves IPC by 1.37% over the original in matched configurations.

title: Modified wave operators for the critical long-range nonlinear Schrödinger equation
authors: Jia Shen, Yifei Wu
abstract: In this paper, we construct modified wave operators for the critical long-range nonlinear Schrödinger equation with final data $\langle x\rangle^s u_+\in L_x^2,\ d/2<s\le2$, for dimensions $d=1,2,3$, and for both defocusing and focusing cases. We impose no smallness, nonvanishing, or spatial derivative assumption. Most previous modified wave operator results require smallness on $\|\widehat u_+\|_{L^\infty}$, analytic final data or smooth amplitude-phase structure, and the large data modified wave operator problem with finite weighted condition is only solved for 1D defocusing equation. We introduce a new perturbation method which successfully applies to both defocusing and focusing signs when $d\le3$. The main ingredient is an improved growth estimate for the linearized flow, obtained by a low--high frequency decomposition. At low frequencies, spatial localization and freezing the coefficients in space lead to a Fuchsian system. The nilpotent structure at the singular point and a Hamiltonian energy estimate give logarithmic growth for this system. At high frequencies, a modified energy for suitable symmetry operator cancels the leading contribution to energy growth.

title: Magic-layer scenario for predicting non-van der Waals two-dimensional materials: The case of double-layer honeycomb structures
authors: Shota Ono
abstract: A magic number is a specific size of a van der Waals (vdW) cluster that shows pronounced stability compared to adjacent sizes, and therefore magic clusters are preferentially formed in experiments. We apply the ``magic-layer'' concept to identify non-vdW two-dimensional (2D) materials that are difficult to exfoliate from their parent 3D crystals. As a case, we study the stability of thin films in III-V, II-VI, I-VII, and Mn-based compounds using first-principles calculations. By calculating excess energies for various thicknesses, we find significant stabilization reflecting the formation of double-layer honeycomb structures at specific thicknesses. The stability measure based on the magic-layer concept can distinguish the experimentally synthesized systems from the experimentally unrealized systems, which serves as a key descriptor for predicting the realization of non-vdW 2D materials.

title: Mixed-Initiative Mining of Root-Cause Analyses into Audit Priors for C/C++ Vulnerability Hunting
authors: Yuhei Kawakoya, Eitaro Shioji, Yuto Otsuki, Makoto Iwamura
abstract: Vulnerability auditing of large C/C++ codebases is constrained by limited review attention. Human auditors and LLM-based agents need operational priors that indicate where to look first and what to suspect, but such priors are rarely available in directly usable form. Rather than proposing a new vulnerability detector, we derive audit-steering artifacts from evidence-backed root-cause analysis (RCA) reports. We introduce two complementary representations: Occurrence Context (OC), a location prior based on file role, function role, and data-structure class; and Vulnerability-Inducing Structural Patterns (VISP), reusable failure-mechanism priors. OC guides where to inspect, while VISP guides what to suspect. On 108 CVEs from Vul4C, OC's parser-based priority ranking, without LLM inference, outperforms generic prioritization baselines with moderate-to-large effect sizes. Packaged as executable SKILLs, OC and VISP form a dual-SKILL workflow that improves audit-relevant broad coverage, defined as match-or-partial findings within ground-truth functions that share the patch's failure mechanism, as assessed by three LLM judges. Across the 108-CVE cohort, dual-SKILL improves function-level broad matches by 5.3 percentage points; gains reach 7.2 points on mid-size projects and 15.0 points on large (1500-4999-line) vulnerable files. These results suggest that RCA-derived priors help direct limited audit attention toward vulnerable code. The agent-coverage evaluation is a single-run operational probe, with one run per commit, characterizing the direction and scale of the effect rather than its precise magnitude.

title: Streaming instabilities and electron transport in electron transpiration cooling
authors: Wushun Zhang, Yinjian Zhao, Weixing Zhou
abstract: Electron transpiration cooling requires emitted electrons to travel through a surrounding plasma, where their relative motion with background electrons can drive streaming instabilities. We investigate these instabilities using particle-in-cell simulations with Monte Carlo collisions in a finite helium plasma. Lower neutral densities show pronounced wave activity, while higher densities give smoother electron distributions. A multifluid model constructed from simulated velocity distributions captures the frequency scale and decay direction in selected cases, but underestimates the separate driving and absorbing responses of electron populations. Distinguishing fast and slow emitted electrons and normalizing the field amplitude by the expanding two-peak length improves the low-wavenumber growth comparison, while discrepancies remain. Spatial growth estimates show that finite propagation distance also limits amplification. Strong late-time current fluctuations can coexist with nearly complete mean anode collection. These findings connect streaming instability to electron transport in the cooling model and show both the usefulness and limitations of a fluid description.

title: LeanWAM: Learning Latent World Action Models from Frozen Video Models
authors: Shaolong Li, Hongze Fu, Joyce Chai, Yinpei Dai
abstract: World action models (WAMs) typically adapt large pretrained video generators to jointly predict future observations and robot actions, incurring substantial training and deployment costs. However, it remains unclear which future representations a policy actually needs and how compactly they can be represented. Our probing study shows that complementary future representations can be compressed into a few tokens while retaining most of their action-decoding performance. Motivated by this finding, we introduce LeanWAM, a latent WAM that transfers video priors from a frozen video generator to a lightweight policy via two-stage training. In the first stage, a Future Extractor compresses observed transitions into 32 predictive tokens. These tokens condition the frozen generator and are jointly shaped by action, RGB, semantic, and geometric supervision, while a compact readout of the generator's hidden states supplies complementary world tokens. The second stage distills both representations into the policy, which learns to predict them from current observations while generating actions. With 1.4B parameters and no large-scale embodied pretraining, LeanWAM outperforms strong vision-language-action (VLA) and WAM baselines on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin~2.0. It predicts an action chunk in 25.1\,ms on an A100 GPU, 12.3--41.5$\times$ faster than representative WAMs. These results demonstrate that compact predictive supervision can transfer video priors to robust and efficient control.

title: Where is the Interface for the AI Harness?
authors: Wafa Johal, Sarah Schombs
abstract: Norman's gulfs of execution and evaluation have guided interaction design for forty years, but both assume a user who is present in the loop. Agentic delegation breaks that assumption: users describe an outcome and leave, while the agent takes hundreds of unseen actions. Starting from a 2026 incident in which a research agent circumvented an access refusal on an Australian government portal and went unnoticed for two months, we argue that delegation opens two new gulfs. The gulf of specification is the gap between what a user wants and their ability to express it, including how the agent should behave in situations nobody foresaw. The gulf of oversight is the gap between what an agent is doing and the user's ability to know, assess, and control it. We argue that both gulfs meet in the harness, the tools, permissions, checks, and loop that surround the model. Harnesses are currently written by developers and hidden from users. We call on HCI to decide which parts of the harness belong to the end-user, which should be visible and adjustable defaults, and which should be built in by design, and to create the interfaces that let ordinary people author and read them.

title: Solving (Vertex-Weighted) Directed Multiway Cut Faster Than $2^n$
authors: Mingyu Xiao
abstract: In the Directed Multiway Cut problem, we are given a directed graph $G=(V,E)$ and a subset $T\subseteq V$, called the terminal set. The aim is to find a minimum-cardinality set $S\subseteq V\setminus T$, such that after deleting $S$, no directed path exists from one terminal to another terminal in the remaining graph. It had been an open question whether \textsc{Directed Multiway Cut} can be solved faster than the trivial running-time bound $O^*(2^{|V|})$. In this paper, we provide a positive answer to this question, presenting an algorithm with a running-time bound $O(1.9967^{|V|})$. The algorithm can also be modified to solve the weighted version (each vertex having a positive weight) in $O^*(1.9985^{|V|})$ time.

title: GreenDynaMix: Thermal-Aware Dynamic Mixed-Precision MoE LLM Inference Systems
authors: Han-Yi Lin, Kieran Griperay, Qiang Zhou, Xiangyu Zhou, Nate Bonacci, Zinachidi Achikeh, Li He, Shaofei Qi, Hongqiang Wang, Jeff Zhang, Tianlong Chen, Pi-Cheng Hsiu, Jingtong Hu
abstract: Sustained Large Language Model (LLM) inference generates significant heat that exacerbates silicon aging and reduces GPU reliability. Because GPU temperature fluctuates continuously with workload intensity and ambient conditions, keeping it in a safe range requires real-time frequency scaling, which inevitably comes at the cost of either throughput or accuracy. To address this tightly coupled challenge, we propose GreenDynaMix, the first runtime system to jointly integrate a DVFS-based thermal manager with a dynamic precision-tuning throughput compensator. A sensitivity-aware allocator leverages intrinsic importance signals from the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) router to assign higher precision to critical experts, preserving accuracy. Experiments on server, desktop, and embedded platforms demonstrate that GreenDynaMix reduces the temperature-induced aging rate of GPUs during LLM inference by 25-33%. Without offline profiling or model retraining, it recovers throughput at a perplexity cost of 0.9-1.6% with 8-bit/4-bit mixed precision, rising to 9.4% where memory forces 4-bit/2-bit.

title: Reproducing History Is Not Enough: Intervention-Level Assurance for LLM-Generated Simulators
authors: Ashraf Abdul-Muumin, Aniruddha Chattopadhyay, Noorbakhsh Golilarz, Kaushik Roy
abstract: Large language models can now write simulation programs of operational processes and workflows. These programs can be reused to answer what-if questions on new records and policies. However, a program that reproduces recorded history can still give wrong answers to what-if questions; requested changes may be applied wrongly, or they may be applied to records other than the ones the question is about, or the program may stop being valid once its policy is revised. Current checks return a pass-or-fail verdict for the whole program, which says little about whether any single answer can be trusted. We propose Vouch, a library that judges whether an answer from a generated simulator can be trusted for the change being asked about. Each what-if question is turned into a structured change, which is checked against the program and the current records. The library also keeps a record of the kinds of change each program has passed or failed, and repeats the relevant tests whenever the program is reused. We apply it to three program-generation platforms, with programs built by five language models, across four domains: manufacturing, IT operations, and pharmacy and loan-application workflows, using independently checked reference answers. Our baselines are the platforms' own checks where such checks exist, an LLM-as-a-judge, and a ReAct agent that can run the program. We measure how many correct answers are trusted, how many are wrongly rejected, how many wrong answers are accepted, and what the checking costs. On programs written by Haiku and Sonnet in one platform, Vouch removes 97.6% of the wrong answers, while still trusting 80.1% of all answers. At equal coverage, it accepts fewer wrong answers than LLM judges built on Claude Haiku. We disclose code and results for reproducibility.

title: Tokenization and Architecture Jointly Allocate Component Roles in Time Series Transformers
authors: Mingyu Kim, Doguk Kim
abstract: Time series transformers have achieved strong forecasting performance, yet it remains unclear which of their components, attention or the feed-forward network (FFN), constructs temporal features, and how tokenization such as patching changes this. We propose a temporal probing framework that uses 15 token-level diagnostic tasks to measure feature construction as the gain in linear decodability of temporal properties from one sub-layer to the next (a matched MLP probe already saturates at the embedding). It targets models whose probed representations are read by a linear forecasting head. Applied to 5 supervised models trained on 8 long-term forecasting benchmarks, it finds that the constructing component is not fixed but allocated by the interaction of tokenization and architecture. Under patch tokenization (PatchTST), the FFN's gain exceeds attention's in probing on all 8 datasets, and its 8-dataset mean is 3.2x attention's. Without attention, the FFN alone reaches nearly the same total gain, both when attention is removed from a trained model and when PatchTST is trained without it, and the retrained model forecasts within a few percent of the full model. In probing, attention dominates under variate tokenization (iTransformer); in CATS, cross-attention is the only input path. In a controlled manipulation of PatchTST, single-scalar tokens (P=1) nearly eliminate the FFN's construction, while one more point per token (P=2) restores it. Our forecasting-side interventions (activation patching, knockout, and training without attention) establish component-level reliance and sufficiency. These results offer a representational reading of prior findings on the gains from patching, the competitiveness of self-attention-free models (TSMixer, PatchMLP), and the distinct role of cross-attention in CATS.

title: SigK: rPPG-based key agreement scheme for mHealth
authors: Yanping Wang, Lin Li, Leo Yu Zhang, Jianfeng Wang, Chao Chen, Kok-Leong Ong, Jun Zhang
abstract: As mobile health advances, the use of biomedical sensors for disease monitoring, diagnosis, and treatment is increasing. These sensors often need to be connected through wireless communication technologies to process physiological information from various body parts effectively. Since the data transmitted in these devices usually contain sensitive personal medical information, it is crucial to establish secure communication between devices. In recent studies, the inter-pulse intervals between heartbeats are often used as the key source. They can be extracted from physiological signals such as photoplethysmogram (PPG) or electrocardiogram (ECG), allowing key agreement schemes without pre-key distribution. However, traditional solutions are based on contact measurement devices (e.g., wristbands, chest straps), which limit their applicability in contactless healthcare scenarios. In this paper, we propose a remote PPG-based key agreement scheme to facilitate secure communication between contactless medical devices. We leverage medical devices equipped with cameras to capture remote PPG signals from human faces, and then utilize the signal's power spectral density and peak-peak interval to establish a key agreement with signals synchronously acquired in the Body Area Network (BAN). We have carried out performance evaluations on three publicly available datasets to demonstrate the feasibility of our proposed scheme. In addition, we have also presented a comprehensive proof of the security of our proposed scheme.

title: BPS baryonic tubes in chiral perturbation theory minimally coupled with electrodynamics and a novel crossover
authors: Fabrizio Canfora, Martín Garrido, Pablo Pais
abstract: We derive a novel first-order BPS system (whose solutions are automatically solutions of the second-order field equations) in chiral perturbation theory (CPT) in $(3+1)$ dimensions. These BPS configurations describe baryonic tubes carrying a chiral current along the tubes themselves. Such baryonic tubes can be either homogeneous or modulated along the $z$-axis. We analyze the leading term in CPT, which is the $SU(2)$ non-linear sigma model minimally coupled to electrodynamics. These exact solutions are qualitatively different from the available analytic description of baryonic tubes since, due to their BPS nature, the positions of the energy-density peaks can be arbitrary. In contrast (in the case of the known solutions in the literature), the energy-density peaks' positions are fixed. We compare these two types of baryonic configurations; the relevant parameter that determines which one is energetically favored is the baryonic charge density: for low densities, the old solutions are favorable, while for high densities these novel BPS tubes are energetically favored. The inclusion of the electromagnetic field (together with the corresponding back-reaction on the baryonic tubes) can also be treated analytically. We discuss the differences in the electromagnetic field distribution between the two regions (low and high baryonic density). The analysis of potential terms for the chiral field is detailed in Appendix B.

title: Phase matching of high-order harmonics driven by a combined coherent and bright squeezed vacuum field
authors: Yaoshun Sun, Shang Ma, Xintong He, Jiaao Cai, Wentao Wang, Mingxuan Li, Xiangyu Tang, Sizuo Luo
abstract: High-order harmonic generation (HHG) driven by non-classical light provides new insights into light-matter interactions and paves the way to quantum attosecond spectroscopy. Achieving phase matching is vital for generating bright HHG sources, while it has received comparatively limited attention in quantum-light-driven HHG. In this work, we investigate the phase matching of HHG driven by an intense coherent field combined with a weak bright squeezed vacuum (BSV) field, using a semiclassical ensemble of coherent-field realizations sampled from the Husimi-$Q$ probability distribution. We reveal the physical mechanism behind the distinct pressure dependence of the harmonic yields for odd, even and half-integer sidebands spectral components, as observed in our previous experiment [arXiv:2607.20941]. The simulations and phase-matching model demonstrate that the BSV-induced perturbation of the electron action phase could introduce an additional sub-cycle phase mismatch, such that the amplitude of sub-cycle bursts could be significantly modified by gas pressure after macroscopic propagation, even when the harmonic yield is near the optimum. The resulting amplitude asymmetry of sub-cycle bursts leads to a significant intensity contrast between half-integer sidebands harmonics, manifesting as distinct pressure dependence of their yields. Our findings reveal the phase-matching mechanism in two-color quantum-light-driven HHG, and suggest opportunities for macroscopic control of the non-classical HHG source.

title: Combinatorial characterizations of the quantum $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ invariant of positive alternating links and 3-braids
authors: Matthew Harper, Joshua O'Connor, José Sánchez Menchén, Angie Wu
abstract: The $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ link polynomial is a higher rank relative of the Jones polynomial which can be studied entirely diagrammatically using Kuperberg's web calculus. Building on the work of Harper and Kalfagianni, we construct formulae for the fourth and fifth coefficients of the quantum $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ link invariant on positive alternating link diagrams in terms of data read from the associated Seifert graph. Then, we give a characterization of the invariant on positive alternating fibered links in terms of elementary symmetric polynomials. We also discuss behavior of our formulae under connected sums. We give formulations for the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ invariant of even powers of the Garside element $Δ_3\in B_3$ and a closed formula for the invariant on positive $3$-braids, resulting in a formula for the invariant on all $3$-braids.
